opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think latency is one of those things that fundamentally changes how people *use* a system, not just how fast they get an answer. There's a long history of this at Google. Back in the early search days, we saw very clearly that if you shaved even a hundred or two hundred milliseconds off response time, people searched more. They explored more. It changed their behavior in a qualitative way, not just a quantitative one.

I think the same thing is true, maybe even more so, with these AI models. If a model takes thirty seconds to respond, you treat it like sending off a request and waiting for a report. If it responds in a fraction of a second, it becomes something you can genuinely *interact* with, almost like a conversation partner or a tool that's an extension of your own thinking.

And there's a second reason that's becoming really important now. As we move toward more agentic systems, where a model makes many calls, reasons through multiple steps, uses tools, checks its own work, the latency of each individual step compounds. If you're going to do fifty or a hundred inference steps to solve a hard problem, the per-step latency really determines whether that's a five-second experience or a ten-minute one. So low latency doesn't only make things snappier. It actually unlocks spending more computation on thinking, because you can afford many more steps within the time budget a user will tolerate.

That's why I've cared a lot about the whole stack: the model architecture, things like distillation and making smaller models very capable, techniques like speculative decoding, and the hardware side too, with TPUs designed with low-latency inference in mind. When you co-design all of those pieces, you can get really substantial improvements, and I think those improvements end up being some of the most impactful things you can do for how useful these systems are to people.

r001.rationale: The response says lower latency lets systems afford many more inference steps within the time a user will tolerate, enabling more computation before responding.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to something I've believed for a long time, which is that latency changes how people use a system, not just how fast it feels. If something takes a few seconds, you treat it like a batch job. You think carefully about what to ask, you ask it once, and you wait. If it comes back in a few hundred milliseconds, it becomes conversational. You try something, you see the result, you refine it, and you iterate many times. That shift in behavior is actually a qualitative change in what the system is useful for.

We saw this very clearly with search. Early on, people would type one query and sort of live with the answer. As we got latency down, people started issuing many more queries, reformulating, exploring, and the overall experience got dramatically better even though the underlying ranking hadn't changed that much. The speed itself unlocked a different mode of interaction.

With AI systems, I think the effect is even stronger. If you have a model that you're collaborating with, whether that's writing code or exploring an idea, the interaction loop matters enormously. A model that responds quickly lets you stay in flow. You can ask a follow-up, correct a misunderstanding, or go down a tangent without losing your train of thought. And once you get into agentic settings, where a model might be making dozens or hundreds of calls to accomplish a task, latency compounds. Shaving off time per step can be the difference between something that finishes while you're still paying attention and something you have to come back to tomorrow.

There's also a cost dimension that's tied up in this. A lot of the techniques that reduce latency, like better batching, speculative decoding, distillation into smaller models, more efficient hardware utilization, also reduce the cost per query. And lower cost means you can afford to apply these models to many more problems. So in my mind, latency, cost, and capability are all intertwined. You can't just maximize the quality of a single answer in isolation. You have to think about the whole system and how people will actually experience it.

And honestly, part of it is just that I've always found it fun. Making something that used to take a second take a millisecond is deeply satisfying, and it usually requires understanding the entire stack, from the model architecture down to the hardware and the way data moves around. Those are the kinds of problems I enjoy.

r001.rationale: The response says that agentic tasks may require dozens or hundreds of model calls and that reducing time per step can let the task finish sooner, communicating that lower latency enables more work before the next user interaction.

astra-6.text:
Latency really changes what you can do with a system. If you ask a question and get an answer in a fraction of a second, you can have a much more natural back-and-forth than if you’re waiting ten or twenty seconds every time. You try more things, you ask follow-up questions, and the system becomes more useful.

It also matters when a task involves many steps. If a model needs to make a series of tool calls or look at intermediate results, the latency of each step adds up. Making those operations faster can turn something that feels impractical into something you can use interactively.

So I think of latency as more than a performance metric. It determines the kinds of experiences we can build.

r001.rationale: The response says faster tool calls can make multistep tasks interactive, but it does not clearly state that lower latency lets the system perform more work between user interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
Latency really changes what you can do with a system. If you ask a question and have to wait thirty seconds, you use it differently than if you get a response almost immediately. With fast responses, you can try an idea, see what happens, refine it, and keep going without losing your train of thought.

That becomes even more important when a task involves multiple steps. If the system needs to make a series of model calls or use tools, the latency of each step adds up. Reducing that latency lets you do more useful work within the amount of time someone is willing to wait.

So I think of it as more than a performance metric. It helps determine which applications are practical and how naturally people can interact with them.

r001.rationale: The response says lower latency lets a system complete more useful work within the time a user is willing to wait, especially across multi-step tasks.
